Hi Anton,
I took a look at your sample project, and it looks like you've found a bug. I've filed it here:
https://github.com/bedatadriven/renjin/issues/102

If you print() the data.frame you've read in, you'll see that Renjin incorrectly converts your date/time column to a numeric vector containing c(2015, 2015,) silently discarding the rest of the string.

I'm doing some work on read.table to address a number of other issues so hope to have a fix for this shortly, but in the meantime, you can work around it by providing a 'colClasses' argument that will avoid the automatic type conversion.

See this blog post for a tutorial on how to use the colClasses argument:

http://www.r-bloggers.com/using-colclasses-to-load-data-more-quickly-in-r/

Best,
Alex

messages.subject: update to the Renjin build system, versioning and a Debian repo
messages.subject_clean: update to the Renjin build system, versioning and a Debian repo
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

we have recently changed how Renjin is build and versioned. Instead of working with Release Candidates and SNAPSHOTS we have now set up Jenkins to build Renjin whenever a change is committed to the master branch in GitHub. We still use semantic versioning but now we use the build number as the patch version. For example, the latest stable build is 0.7.1520. You will see this version mentioned when you use the CLI.

To make it easier to use the very latest version in your Maven projects, you can set the version to RELEASE in your POM file. The README on GitHub has been updated to reflect this: https://github.com/bedatadriven/renjin

Finally, we have also set up a Debian repository for the command line version of Renjin. Execute

deb http://nexus.bedatadriven.com/content/repositories/renjin-release/ ./

to enable the repository in a Debian-based linux distribution. Then execute sudo apt-get install renjin to install the package. After it has been installed, you can type "renjin" in your terminal to start the command line interface of the interpreter.

Maarten-Jan

Hi Anton,

I don´t know if you are still struggling with this question, but I seem to have found a better solution to reading csv files.  For method read.csv you can pass a parameter called 'colClasses' as follows:

read.csv("../test/reputation.csv", sep = "#", header = false, colClasses: c("character", "numeric", "numeric", "character", "character",
      "numeric"))

In this case, I´m saying that the first column should be read as character, the second as numeric, etc.  My reputation.csv file has an IP address on the first colum of the form "254.123.65.11" and when read by read.csv without the colClasses param, the first column only has 254.123 as if it were a number.  With colClasses and 'character' the whole IP is read.

Hope this helps.

Cheers,

Right, so if you were in Java land, you would write:

long timeInMillis = trades.get(2).getOrderOpenTime().getTime()

which gives you a unix timestamp: the number of milliseconds since Jan 1 1970

Renjin understands 'long' values, it doesn't (currently) understand anything specific about java.util.Date objects, other than the fact that's a java object with properties.

So you can write in R:

timeInMillis <- trades[[2]]$orderOpenTime$time

This in turn is value you can convert to an R date object using the expression

 as.POSIXct(timeInMillis/1000, origin="1970-01-01")

Does that make sense?

Best,
Alex
